processes: Assigning each element a unique box on the table
Keeping element identity fixed through reactions
Pairing with atomic mass on the element card
plainLanguageExplanation: The atomic number is the number of protons in an element's atoms. It is the most important number in chemistry because it is the element's identity: an element with atomic number 6 is carbon, with atomic number 8 it is oxygen, with 79 it is gold. Every element has its own unique atomic number, and no two elements share one. The periodic table is organized using this number — the elements are arranged from left to right in order of increasing atomic number, starting with hydrogen (1) and running up through the table. On each element's card in the periodic table, the atomic number is the small number usually printed at the top. It is also the number of electrons in a neutral atom of the element, because a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons. The atomic number never changes during chemical reactions — atoms can lose or gain electrons and become ions, but they keep their protons, so they keep their identity.

keyFacts.label: What it counts
keyFacts.value: The number of protons in an element's atoms

keyFacts.label: Identity
keyFacts.value: It is the element's unique ID — atomic number 6 is carbon, 8 is oxygen

keyFacts.label: Order
keyFacts.value: Elements are listed on the table in order of increasing atomic number

keyFacts.label: Electrons
keyFacts.value: In a neutral atom, the atomic number also equals the number of electrons

keyFacts.label: Fixed
keyFacts.value: It never changes in chemical reactions — protons stay put

whyItMatters: The atomic number is the key that unlocks the entire periodic table. Once you know that each element is defined by its proton count and that the table is arranged by that count, you can find any element, predict whether atoms of the same kind are truly the same, and understand why the table's layout works the way it does.
didYouKnow: Because the atomic number counts protons and the periodic table is ordered by it, element 118, oganesson, has 118 protons — and every new element discovered is simply the next number up.
compareReason: Both numbers sit on every element card, but the atomic number is a clean whole proton count that names the element, while atomic mass is a decimal average that includes neutrons — comparing them shows what each number really means.
